## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so dev success can't tell us yet whether the network or the training is the problem. The default recipe gives only 131k steps, which is 32 updates of 4,096 samples. That is probably too few samples for a policy over about 257 actions to learn exact builds of 6–16 bricks. Following the suggested split for round 1, the three candidates are: (a) a recipe-only change, with ppo_epochs 2 for about 1.86× the samples, a longer gamma and a higher GAE lambda for the end-of-episode +1 bonus; (b) a network about as costly as the start (r≈1.07) with two residual 3×3 blocks, global context fed into each block and the action head, and near-uniform starting logits; (c) both together. I'll judge them by mean training success while dev success stays at 0. I avoided ppo_epochs 1 because it gives 3.25× the steps, and we don't yet know whether environment time would break the 900-second limit.

### Round 2
All six seeds scored 0 on both dev and training success. So the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. Neither change helped: about 1.75× more samples (2 epochs, gamma 0.97) and global context did nothing. Time is not a limit: about 66 s of the 900 s allowed.

My guess at the cause is the reward. A brick covering 3 target cells and 1 extra cell earns net positive reward, so PPO can settle on greedy, sloppy filling. The +1 exact-build bonus is the only thing pushing against that, and gamma 0.95–0.97 discounts it heavily.

Two fixes follow:
1. A longer horizon (gamma 0.99 or higher) with as many samples as possible (ppo_epochs 1, about 400k steps).
2. A head that can detect an exact fit at each footprint. Its min, max and average pooling should see the per-cell, per-layer stem features directly through a skip, instead of only features blurred by the 3×3 convolutions.

The results will be ranked by training success.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on both dev and training success, across both seeds. So the problem is learning itself, not generalisation. The recipe changes (1–2 epochs giving up to 405k steps, gamma 0.97–0.995, entropy 0.003) did nothing. The network changes (global context, a skip into the footprint head) also did nothing, and so did combining them. Runs take about 65 s, so time is not a limit; the FLOP budget is. Every network so far mixes all height layers into 2D channels with a few convolutions. To judge a placement, the network must find where the brick lands (the highest filled cell under it), check that the target has those cells at that layer, and check that nothing needed is sealed underneath. Learning that from layer-entangled channels may be too hard to bootstrap. One gap I haven't tested: all runs used about 1.6k–4k gradient steps. Next I'll try a per-layer, layer-equivariant head, and many small-minibatch updates.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success. That covers recipe changes (1, 2 and 4 epochs; gamma 0.95 to 0.995; entropy 0.003 to 0.01; lr 1e-3 to 1.5e-3; up to 405k steps) and three architectures (residual nets with global context, a skip head, a layer-equivariant head). Even sampled training never builds a target exactly. A dense reward should get small 6-brick designs right some of the time, so this pattern points to one of three causes: the world behaves differently from its description (for example a different anchor convention or drop rule), the optimisation is unstable, or the network can't predict where a brick lands. All trials ran well inside the time limit (60 to 170 seconds). Three things are untested. The legality mask carries landing and height information, and no trial has used it as a learned input. No trial has used a low learning rate (3e-4), and no trial has used a learned per-type head with a 3×3 kernel that doesn't depend on the anchor convention. No architecture with global attention has been tried.
